root.claim: A deterministic multitape Turing machine multiplies $n$-bit integers in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ time with $\kappa=2^{-182}$.
root.method: reduce to convolution, accelerate transforms by two network-based tape procedures, then recover the product

motivation.text: Beating n log n needs a power saving in the log factor, which requires cheaper transform levels (S3) inside the standard multiplication-by-convolution reduction (S2, S4) with exact recovery (S5).

root.salient: $\kappa=2^{-182}$ is an astronomically small exponent; it is the product of the saving exponents from the recursions, so only a tiny power of log is saved.

children.claim: A fixed finite network with nested subspaces attached to gates, built from three-element subsets with gather/scatter and cancelling auxiliary wires, makes the total number $s$ of smaller calls satisfy $s<Wm$.
A call at parameter $mf$ uses $s$ calls at parameter $f$ on volume $V/W$ each, so cost per volume grows by $s/W<m$ per multiplication of the parameter by $m$, a power saving.
children.salient: The saving is a strict inequality $s/W<m$ that holds uniformly at every recursion level, which turns into a power of the parameter rather than a constant factor.

children.claim: The digit convolution reduces, by a chain of changes of problem and representation, to convolution over $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$.
children.method: chain of reductions: prime cyclic axes, power-of-two axes, polynomial ring

motivation.text: The fast tape procedures and synthetic transforms apply only to power-of-two axes with negacyclic ring coordinate, while the digit convolution has no such shape.

children.claim: The radix-digit list is placed on a product of cyclic axes of distinct prime lengths by a Chinese-remainder address map that preserves convolution.
Gaussian resampling expresses each prime-length Fourier transform through a power-of-two tensor transform with source and target permutations retained.
Bluestein's chirp identity turns the middle transform into a normalized cyclic convolution multiplied by chirp phases.
A last-coordinate phase twist turns a cyclic coordinate into a polynomial coordinate modulo $y^r+1$; removing the twist restores the cyclic wrap.
Convolution over the remaining axes is computed over $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ by forward synthetic transforms, pointwise ring products and the opposite transform.

motivation.text: This is the convolution theorem: transforms turn convolution into pointwise products, and the ring makes twiddle multiplications shifts.

children.claim: Synthetic polynomial transforms use powers of $y$ as roots of unity, so twiddles are signed shifts, and two forward transforms retain one frequency order through the pointwise product.
Pointwise polynomial products in the ring are computed by signed packing (Kronecker substitution) and the standard $O(n\log n)$ multiplier as an ordinary subroutine.
The approximate transforms recover the exact integer product, and the total cost is $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$.
children.method: bound the rounding error below 1/2 and then add up costs

motivation.text: Rounding to the nearest integer is exact only once the error is below 1/2; the cost is a sum over steps controlled by the chosen parameters.
